text:
Microsoft's Recall feature became a privacy scandal in 2024 because it was initially designed as an AI "memory" tool that took screenshots of the user’s screen every few seconds and stored them locally to make them searchable [Source: ev-1]. Security researchers, including Kevin Beaumont, demonstrated that these screenshots were stored unencrypted (in plaintext) within a local SQLite database, contradicting Microsoft’s claims of encryption [Source: ev-1]. Furthermore, the system captured sensitive content visible on the screen—such as passwords, health data, and private messages—by default, making this information accessible to any process running under the same user account [Source: ev-1]. This combination of a default-on recorder for all on-screen activity with flawed security assurances led privacy regulators, such as the Irish Data Protection Commission and the UK Information Commissioner's Office, to raise questions, while the Washington State Attorney General opened an investigation [Source: ev-1].

To address these concerns, Microsoft delayed the feature in June 2024 and subsequently reversed its default settings [Source: ev-1]. The relaunched version is now opt-in (default OFF) rather than enabled by default [Source: ev-1]. Additionally, accessing the timeline now requires Windows Hello authentication and presence detection, and the system explicitly excludes incognito mode and DRM content from capture [Source: ev-1]. Although this revised, opt-in version reached general availability on Copilot+ PCs in 2025, the initial controversy permanently shaped privacy discussions surrounding AI PCs [Source: ev-1].
